extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, geologists, and educated general readers interested in physical geography and volcanology
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century scientific exposition describing the origin, classification, and physical controls of earthquakes, thermal springs, mud-volcanoes (salses), craters of elevation, and true volcanoes, with observational examples worldwide. The text synthesizes observational rules and causal relations used to interpret geothermal and volcanic phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a true volcano
rubrics_metrics.description: A volcano, properly so called, exists only where a permanent connection is established between the interior of the earth and the atmosphere, and the reaction of the interior on the surface then continues during long periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes true volcanoes from transient or one-time upheavals; permanence of the conduit/connection is the key diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between salses (mud volcanoes) and true volcanoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Salses disengage little else but carbureted hydrogen, together with bitumen and other products of the distillation of coal, and pour forth no other torrents except of mud or argillaceous materials mixed up with water; they are not true volcanoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salses may show an initial violent explosion of fire but commonly enter a long peaceful state with cold mud emissions; their products (mud, hydrocarbons, bitumen) and lack of lava flows distinguish them from igneous volcanoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance and character of carbonic acid exhalations (mofettes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhalations of carbonic acid ('mofettes') are to be considered the most important of all gaseous emanations with respect to their number and the amount of their effusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mofettes are often the last efforts of volcanic activity in or near earlier volcanic foci (examples: Eifel, Lake of Laach, Wehr valley, Western Bohemia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature of springs as function of origin and mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: The temperature of springs depends on the temperature of the stratum in which they take their rise, on the specific heat of the soil, and on the quantity and temperature of the meteoric water, which itself varies with origin (rain, snow, hail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of isogeothermal lines from flowing springs is complicated by blending of waters from different heights and depths; surface mixing obscures deep-source temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth required for spring temperature invariability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold springs can indicate the mean atmospheric temperature only when unmixed with waters from great depths or mountain descent, and when they have passed through a long course at a depth from the surface equal in our latitudes to 40 or 60 feet, and, according to Boussingault, to about one foot in the equinoctial regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These depths mark where hourly, daily, and monthly atmospheric changes cease to affect ground temperature; Boussingault's tropical result emphasizes much shallower invariability in the tropics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of thermal springs and role of depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Hot permanent springs may have sources many thousands of feet deep; if terrestrial heat is the cause, rocks influence spring temperature by different heat capacities and conducting powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: springs issuing from granite recorded at 194.5°F and from basalt at 205.5°F, suggesting sources ~7140 feet deep (above two miles) based on the known law of increase of heat with depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and temperature relation of the hottest permanent springs
rubrics_metrics.description: The hottest of all permanent springs (between 203 degrees and 209 degrees) are likewise, in a most remarkable degree, the purest, and such as hold in solution the smallest quantity of mineral substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their mineral content and thermal stability vary with temperature class; springs between 122 and 165°F have shown long-term invariability of heat and mineral contents over decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical signatures of volcanic activity states
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the gaseous compounds of sulphur, sulphurous acid appears to predominate chiefly in volcanoes possessing a certain degree of activity, while sulphureted hydrogen has been most frequently perceived among those in a dormant condition; abundant exhalations of sulphuric acid have been noticed chiefly in extinct volcanoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dumas' explanation: sulphureted hydrogen at temperatures above 100°F (better near 190°F) encountering porous bodies can be catalytically transformed into water, sulphuric acid, and sulphur, explaining sulphate deposits in extinct volcanic districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of travertine and travertine geomorphology
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermal water, when impregnated with carbonic acid and sulphurous gases, are continually forming horizontally ranged strata of limestone (travertine) or conical elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travertine deposits can preserve remains of former vegetation (example: Van Diemen's Land travertine contains remains of vegetation no longer extant); travertine represents a depositional product of thermal waters distinct from lava.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mud-volcano (salse) lifecycle and eruptive behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Mud volcanoes, after a first violent explosion of fire (not equally common to all), present an image of uninterrupted but weak activity; the communication with deep, high-temperature strata is soon closed and subsequent emissions are often cold mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and recent examples (Jokmali, Baklichli, Monte Ziblo, Macalubi) show flames, loud gas development, torn rock masses, and long intervals of quiescence lasting centuries; gases vary (hydrogen + naphtha, carbonic acid, almost pure nitrogen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crater of elevation versus eruptive craters
rubrics_metrics.description: Craters of elevation are produced by elastic vapors elevating separate portions of the earth's crust into dome-shaped unopened masses of feldspathic trachyte and dolerite; they open no permanent channel of communication with the interior and ordinarily manifest no eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such craters may be filled with water, form lakes, and their origin is not confined to any specific rock type; they differ from eruptive volcanoes which have persistent conduits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between volcano height and eruption frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions are more frequent in low than in elevated volcanoes; if the focus of volcanoes be at an equal depth below the surface, a greater force must be required where fused masses must be raised to much higher elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational series (Stromboli low and active; Cotopaxi high and infrequent) illustrate the law; exceptions occur when the permanence of the conduit varies and when channels close temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for lateral fissure eruptions when flanks offer less resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions from the crater are very unusual in many mountains, generally occurring from lateral fissures whenever the sides of the upheaved mountain were least able, from their configuration and position, to offer any resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical observations (Aetna in the 16th century) show lateral fissure eruptions when crater outlet resistance is high; mechanical configuration of mountain flanks influences eruption loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of volcanic/tectonic surface expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The reaction of the interior of the earth on its external surface is exhibited in a range of phenomena: earthquakes, thermal aqueous and gaseous springs, mud volcanoes, dome-shaped trachytic rocks without openings, opening of rocks as craters of elevation, and elevation of permanent volcanoes with lava streams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification requires careful distinction between these related but distinct phenomena and recognition that they represent gradations of the same interior-surface interaction.
